meta.name: Google Cloud Professional Machine Learning Engineer
meta.notes: Initial GCP PMLE pack — covers Vertex AI Training (custom vs AutoML), Feature Store, Pipelines, Model Monitoring (training-serving skew vs prediction drift), Vertex Explainable AI, online vs batch endpoints, BigQuery ML, Vertex AI Vizier hyperparameter tuning, distributed training strategies, TFRecord storage, Dataflow preprocessing, and responsible AI bias mitigation. Balanced answer key (3/3/3/3 across A/B/C/D).

questions.question: Your team needs a single managed Google Cloud platform that supports the entire ML lifecycle — labeling, training (both AutoML and custom), hyperparameter tuning, model registry, online and batch prediction, and pipeline orchestration. Which service should you standardize on?
options: BigQuery ML — SQL-based model training on warehouse data
Dataproc — managed Hadoop and Spark clusters
Cloud Composer — managed Apache Airflow for workflow orchestration
Vertex AI — the unified, managed end-to-end ML platform
questions.explanation: Vertex AI is Google Cloud's unified, end-to-end managed ML platform. It consolidates AutoML, custom training, Feature Store, Pipelines, Model Registry, Endpoints (online + batch), Explainable AI, Vizier hyperparameter tuning and Model Monitoring in one place. BigQuery ML is for SQL-based modeling inside BigQuery only, Dataproc is for Hadoop/Spark analytics, and Cloud Composer is a generic Airflow orchestrator — none of them is the unified ML platform.

questions.question: A data analyst with strong SQL skills but limited Python experience needs to train a regression model directly on a 2 TB BigQuery table without exporting the data. Which approach minimizes effort and data movement?
options: Export the table to Cloud Storage as CSV, then train with Vertex AI custom container jobs
Spin up a Dataproc cluster and train with Spark MLlib reading via the BigQuery connector
Use BigQuery ML and run a CREATE MODEL statement that trains in place on BigQuery
Stream the rows through Pub/Sub and train an online model with Vertex AI Workbench
questions.explanation: BigQuery ML lets analysts train models with familiar CREATE MODEL SQL syntax, executing inside BigQuery so no data is moved. It supports linear/logistic regression, boosted trees, ARIMA Plus, k-means, matrix factorization and can import or export to Vertex AI. Exporting to GCS for Vertex AI custom training, running Spark MLlib on Dataproc, or streaming through Pub/Sub all require Python and add unnecessary infrastructure for this SQL-centric scenario.

questions.question: Two teams keep computing the same customer-recency and 30-day-purchase features from raw logs, leading to subtle differences between training and serving. You need a central, low-latency store that reuses identical feature definitions across both pipelines. Which Vertex AI capability fits best?
options: Vertex AI Pipelines — DAG orchestration for ML workflows
Vertex AI Feature Store — managed registry and online/offline feature serving
Vertex AI Model Registry — versioned catalog of trained models
Vertex AI Workbench — managed JupyterLab notebooks
questions.explanation: Vertex AI Feature Store centralizes feature definitions and serves the same values to both training (offline, batch reads) and online prediction (low-latency lookups), eliminating training-serving skew caused by duplicated transformation code. Pipelines orchestrate workflows, the Model Registry catalogs trained models, and Workbench provides notebooks — none of them is a feature store.

questions.question: After deploying a fraud-detection model to a Vertex AI endpoint, you notice gradually degrading precision. The input feature distributions in production have shifted compared to the training data, but the ground-truth labels arrive weeks later. Which Model Monitoring signal should you configure to detect this issue early?
options: Training-serving skew — compares production inputs to the training dataset
Feature attribution drift only — ranks SHAP attribution changes per request
Endpoint latency alerts in Cloud Monitoring — fires when p95 exceeds the SLO
Prediction drift — compares the live input distribution to a recent production baseline
questions.explanation: Vertex AI Model Monitoring distinguishes two distribution-shift signals. Training-serving skew compares serving inputs against the original training data and assumes the training distribution is still the ground truth. Prediction drift compares the current serving distribution against a recent serving baseline and is the right signal when the world is evolving over time and you want to catch gradual change. Feature attribution drift is complementary but not the primary input-distribution detector, and latency alerts say nothing about data quality.

questions.question: A regulated insurer must reproduce, on demand, the exact data, code and hyperparameters used to train any production model — and run that training the same way each month with versioned artifacts. Which Vertex AI service should orchestrate the end-to-end workflow?
options: Cloud Functions triggered from Cloud Storage object-finalize events
Vertex AI Pipelines — managed Kubeflow Pipelines with metadata lineage tracking
Cloud Run jobs invoked from a Cloud Scheduler cron entry
BigQuery scheduled queries chained through saved query history
questions.explanation: Vertex AI Pipelines runs Kubeflow Pipelines (or TFX) workflows on a managed, serverless backend and automatically records every artifact, parameter and execution in Vertex ML Metadata — giving the lineage and reproducibility regulators require. Cloud Functions and Cloud Run jobs can run code on a trigger but do not provide ML-aware artifact tracking; BigQuery scheduled queries are SQL-only and do not orchestrate training, evaluation and deployment as a typed DAG.

questions.question: A retail recommender must respond to web requests with personalized suggestions in under 200 ms. A separate weekly job needs to score 80 million users with the same model and write the results to BigQuery. How should you deploy this model in Vertex AI?
options: Deploy to a Vertex AI endpoint for online prediction; use the same model for batch prediction jobs against the BigQuery source
Deploy only an online endpoint and call it from a Dataflow pipeline once per user every week
Run a Vertex AI batch prediction job for every web request and cache the results in Memorystore
Export the model to TensorFlow.js and run all inference in the browser to bypass the endpoint
questions.explanation: Vertex AI distinguishes online prediction (a deployed endpoint backing a low-latency HTTP API, ideal for the 200 ms web path) from batch prediction (a job that reads a BigQuery or GCS input and writes predictions back without a deployed endpoint, ideal for the weekly 80 M-user score). One registered model in the Model Registry can back both — there is no need to invent per-request batch jobs, fan out an endpoint with Dataflow, or push the model into the browser.

questions.question: Your model approves or denies loan applications and must produce, per request, the contribution of each input feature to the score so adjudicators can justify decisions. Which Vertex AI feature provides per-prediction feature attributions for tabular models?
options: Vertex AI Vizier — a black-box hyperparameter tuning service
Cloud DLP — detection and redaction of sensitive data
Vertex Explainable AI — sampled Shapley and Integrated Gradients attributions
Vertex AI Matching Engine — high-scale approximate nearest-neighbor search
questions.explanation: Vertex Explainable AI returns per-feature attributions for every prediction using methods such as sampled Shapley (tabular AutoML and custom models), Integrated Gradients and XRAI (deep models). It is the right primitive for justifying individual decisions. Vizier tunes hyperparameters, DLP redacts sensitive data, and Matching Engine is a vector search service — none of them produces per-prediction attributions.

questions.question: You must train a deep image classifier on 100 GB of labeled photos as fast as possible, with as little code change as possible from your existing single-GPU TensorFlow script. Which distributed-training strategy should you use on Vertex AI custom training?
options: tf.distribute.MirroredStrategy on one multi-GPU machine — synchronous data parallelism across local GPUs
tf.distribute.ParameterServerStrategy across 20 CPU workers — asynchronous parameter updates
A custom Python loop that shards data across Cloud Functions invocations
tf.distribute.experimental.CentralStorageStrategy across regional Cloud Storage buckets
questions.explanation: For a single, dense deep-learning model that fits in GPU memory, MirroredStrategy on a single multi-GPU machine gives synchronous all-reduce data parallelism with essentially no code change — wrap model creation in `strategy.scope()` and Keras handles the rest. ParameterServerStrategy targets very large sparse models or huge clusters and adds async-update complexity, Cloud Functions are not built for long GPU training jobs, and CentralStorageStrategy across regional buckets is not a real distribution strategy.

questions.question: You are tuning seven hyperparameters of a custom model and want Google to use Bayesian optimization to converge on strong settings with fewer training trials than a manual grid search. Which Vertex AI capability should you call?
options: Vertex AI Vizier — black-box optimization service exposed via hyperparameter tuning jobs
Vertex AI Feature Store — online and offline feature serving
Vertex AI TensorBoard — visualization of training metrics
Vertex AI Model Registry — versioned catalog of trained models
questions.explanation: Vertex AI Vizier is Google's black-box optimization service; in Vertex AI it powers hyperparameter tuning jobs that use Bayesian (and other) search algorithms to find good hyperparameters in far fewer trials than grid or random search. Feature Store serves features, TensorBoard visualizes metrics, and the Model Registry catalogs models — none of them performs hyperparameter optimization.

questions.question: You have 8 TB of raw JSON logs that you want to convert into a sharded, compressed format that TensorFlow input pipelines can stream efficiently and shuffle across workers. Which combination minimizes preprocessing latency at training time?
options: Keep the JSON files in Cloud Storage and read them line-by-line with tf.data.TextLineDataset
Load every record into a Cloud SQL table and read with the SQLAlchemy adapter
Preprocess with Dataflow and write sharded TFRecord files to Cloud Storage; consume with tf.data.TFRecordDataset and interleave()
Import the data into BigQuery and use the legacy SQL EXPORT statement during each epoch
questions.explanation: The Google-recommended pattern for large TensorFlow training jobs is to preprocess once with Dataflow into sharded TFRecord files on Cloud Storage, then stream them at training time with `tf.data.TFRecordDataset` plus `interleave` and `prefetch`. TFRecords are a compact, protobuf-based, easily-shardable format optimized for sequential reads. JSON line scans, Cloud SQL fan-out and per-epoch BigQuery exports all add latency and cost per training step.

questions.question: A model that scores resumes is found to under-rank candidates from one demographic group. Before retraining, you want to measure whether the model satisfies a fairness criterion such as equal opportunity across protected groups. Which approach is most appropriate within Google Cloud's responsible-AI tooling?
options: Drop the protected attribute from the training set and assume the model is now fair
Use Vertex Explainable AI together with a fairness analysis (e.g., the What-If Tool or sliced evaluation) to compare per-group metrics such as true-positive rates
Increase the learning rate so the model converges to a more uniform output distribution
Switch from AutoML to a custom model — custom models are inherently fair
questions.explanation: Responsible-AI practice on Google Cloud is to evaluate slices of the data per protected group and compare metrics (true-positive rate, false-positive rate, calibration). Vertex Explainable AI and the What-If Tool support this kind of sliced/fairness analysis, and Vertex AI Model Evaluation reports per-slice metrics. Simply dropping the protected attribute does not remove bias (proxy features remain), tweaking the learning rate has no relationship to fairness, and AutoML vs. custom is unrelated to whether a model is fair.

questions.question: A data-science team prefers JupyterLab and wants a fully managed development environment on Google Cloud with pre-installed TensorFlow and PyTorch, access to GPUs, and built-in connectors to BigQuery and Cloud Storage — without managing the underlying VM lifecycle themselves. Which service should they use?
options: App Engine flexible environment with a custom Jupyter Docker image
Compute Engine VM with a manually installed Anaconda distribution
Cloud Run serving a stateless Jupyter container behind an HTTPS endpoint
Vertex AI Workbench — managed JupyterLab notebooks integrated with Vertex AI services
questions.explanation: Vertex AI Workbench provides fully managed (and user-managed) JupyterLab instances with pre-built TensorFlow, PyTorch and CUDA images, optional GPUs, idle shutdown, and one-click BigQuery and Cloud Storage browsers. It is the recommended notebook environment for Vertex AI. App Engine Flex and Cloud Run are stateless application platforms not designed as interactive notebooks, and a raw Compute Engine VM puts OS, drivers and lifecycle back on the team.
